notes.front: What is a Prometheus client library?
notes.back: A library in a given language that implements the Prometheus metric types, letting you define and expose internal metrics via an HTTP endpoint.
notes.explanation: The page says to add instrumentation through one before you can monitor your services, though if none suits, you may implement one of the exposition formats yourself.
notes.example: Like a translator built into your code, turning your own counts and measurements into the format Prometheus expects to scrape.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Client libraries

notes.front: What is direct instrumentation?
notes.back: Instrumentation added inline as part of a program's own source code, using a client library.
notes.explanation: That's the contrast with an exporter, which pulls metrics from a separate system rather than living inside that system's own code.
notes.example: Like a factory recording its own output on the production line itself, rather than a separate inspector counting from outside.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Glossary, "Direct instrumentation"

notes.front: What is cardinality, in the context of a Prometheus metric's labels?
notes.back: How many distinct label sets a metric has, since each unique labelset is its own additional time series with its own resource cost.
notes.explanation: As a general guideline, the docs suggest keeping a metric's cardinality below 10, with only a handful across a whole system allowed to exceed that.
notes.example: Like a spreadsheet growing one new row for every unique combination of columns: more distinct combinations means more rows to store.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Do not overuse labels"

notes.front: What is an exporter?
notes.back: A binary running alongside the application you want metrics from, which exposes Prometheus metrics, commonly by converting a non-Prometheus format into one.
notes.explanation: Exporters exist for cases where instrumenting a system directly isn't feasible, such as HAProxy or Linux system stats.
notes.example: Like a translator standing beside a foreign-language speaker, converting their words into a language the audience understands.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Glossary, "Exporter"

notes.front: What is the Node exporter?
notes.back: The Node/system metrics exporter: an official exporter, listed under “Hardware related” in the exporters list.
notes.explanation: It's the standard source for machine-level metrics, which is why the docs say other exporters should drop machine metrics they'd otherwise duplicate.
notes.example: Like a building's own facilities monitor, reporting on the building itself rather than on any one tenant inside it.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exporters and integrations, "Hardware related"

notes.front: What is a collector?
notes.back: A part of an exporter that represents a set of metrics: a single metric for direct instrumentation, or many when pulling metrics from another system.
notes.explanation: Custom collectors are what let an exporter's Collect() method build fresh metrics on every scrape, instead of maintaining long-lived state.
notes.example: Like one gauge on a control panel, grouping the readings for one particular subsystem out of the whole panel.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Glossary, "Collector"

notes.front: What is the Pushgateway?
notes.back: An intermediary service that persists the most recent push of metrics from batch jobs, so Prometheus can scrape them after they terminate.
notes.explanation: It exists because a job that has already exited can't be pulled from directly; the Pushgateway holds the result until Prometheus next scrapes it.
notes.example: Like a parcel locker: the sender drops the parcel off and leaves, and the courier collects it on the next round.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Glossary, "Pushgateway"

notes.front: What does the experimental info() function do?
notes.back: For each series in v, it finds matching info series and adds their data (non-identifying) labels onto that series.
notes.explanation: It's built to work with info metrics such as build info, letting queries pull in extra labels like a version string without redesigning the base metric.
notes.example: Like stapling a supplier's extra product details onto your own inventory sheet, matched by the same product code.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Functions, "info()"

notes.front: What are two of the official Prometheus client library languages?
notes.back: Any two of: Go, Java or Scala, Node.js, Python, Ruby, Rust.
notes.explanation: Beyond these, there are also unofficial third-party client libraries for languages such as C, C++, Perl and Elixir.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Client libraries

notes.front: What is an online-serving system, as one of Prometheus's three types of service to monitor?
notes.back: One where a human or another system is expecting an immediate response, such as most database and HTTP requests.
notes.explanation: It's contrasted with offline-processing and batch jobs, where no one is actively waiting on the result.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Online-serving systems"

notes.front: What characterises offline processing, as one of Prometheus's three types of service to monitor?
notes.back: No one is actively waiting for a response, batching of work is common, and there may be multiple stages of processing.
notes.explanation: For each stage, the docs suggest tracking items in, items in progress, the last time something was processed and items sent out; a heartbeat item passed through every stage then shows how long items take to get through.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Offline processing"

notes.front: Batch jobs are distinguished from offline processing by the fact that they {{c1::do not run continuously}}, which makes scraping them difficult.
notes.explanation: The docs say a batch job’s key metrics are gauges that should be pushed to a Pushgateway.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Batch jobs"

notes.front: What are the key metrics for an online-serving system?
notes.back: The number of queries performed, errors, and latency. The number of in-progress requests can also be useful.
notes.explanation: The docs also suggest being consistent about whether queries are counted when they start or when they end, favouring "when they end".
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Online-serving systems"

notes.front: A service handles both HTTP requests and calls out to a downstream database. Should it be monitored only on the client side, or on both sides?
notes.back: Both. Online-serving systems should be monitored on both client and server side; different behaviour on the two sides is useful for debugging.
notes.explanation: If a service has many clients, though, it's not practical to track every one individually, so clients have to rely on their own stats.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Online-serving systems"

notes.front: The key metric of a batch job is {{c1::the last time it succeeded}}.
notes.explanation: It's also useful to track how long each major stage took, the overall runtime, and the last time the job completed (successful or failed).
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Batch jobs"

notes.front: A batch job runs every 5 minutes. Should it stay a Pushgateway-fed batch job, or be converted into a daemon handled as offline processing?
notes.back: The docs suggest converting it into a daemon: for batch jobs running more often than every 15 minutes, consider this instead.
notes.explanation: The 15 minutes is the docs’ own example (“say, more often than every 15 minutes”), not a hard limit.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Batch jobs"

notes.front: What should a library that accesses an outside resource, such as the network or disk, track at a minimum?
notes.back: The overall query count, errors (if errors are possible), and latency.
notes.explanation: It should provide this with no extra configuration required from the library's own users.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Libraries"

notes.front: As a general rule, what should accompany every line of logging code?
notes.back: A counter that gets incremented, so you can see how often a given log message has happened and for how long.
notes.explanation: For several closely related log lines in the same function, it can sometimes make sense to increment a single shared counter for all of them.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Logging"

notes.front: What should generally accompany a failure counter, according to the docs' guidance on failures?
notes.back: Some other metric representing the total number of attempts, so the failure ratio is easy to calculate.
notes.explanation: Every failure should increment a counter, and it may also bubble up to a more general error counter depending on how the code is structured.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Failures"

notes.front: For a threadpool, what are the key metrics the docs recommend tracking?
notes.back: Queued requests, threads in use, total threads, tasks processed, and how long they took; also how long tasks waited in the queue.
notes.explanation: Together these cover both the pool's current load and how efficiently it's working through it.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Threadpools"

notes.front: What are the key metrics for a cache?
notes.back: Total queries, hits, overall latency, plus the query count, errors and latency of the online-serving system the cache sits in front of.
notes.explanation: That last part means a cache's metrics don't stand alone: they're read alongside the system it's fronting.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Caches"

notes.front: A custom metrics collector exports how long its own collection took. Should that duration be a gauge, or a summary/histogram?
notes.back: A gauge. That's one of two acceptable cases for a duration as a gauge, the other being batch job durations.
notes.explanation: In both cases the value describes just that one particular push or scrape, not a series of durations to be aggregated over time.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Collectors"

notes.front: When you have multiple metrics you want to add, average or sum together, what does the docs' guidance recommend instead of separate metrics?
notes.back: Usually, one metric with labels rather than several separately named metrics.
notes.explanation: That's why http_responses_total{code="500"} is preferred over a separate http_responses_500_total metric.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Use labels"

notes.front: A team has separate metrics http_responses_500_total and http_responses_403_total. Following the docs' guidance, how should these be restructured?
notes.back: As one metric, http_responses_total, with a code label for the HTTP response code, processed as one in rules and graphs.
notes.explanation: As a rule of thumb, no part of a metric name should ever be procedurally generated; a label is what that value belongs in instead.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Use labels"

notes.front: As a general guideline, the docs suggest keeping a metric's cardinality below {{c1::10}}, with only a handful across a whole system allowed to exceed it.
notes.explanation: The vast majority of a system's metrics, by this guideline, should have no labels at all.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Do not overuse labels"

notes.front: A metric adds a per-user quota label across 10,000 users on 10,000 nodes, reaching tens of millions of series. What does the guidance say to do?
notes.back: Too much for Prometheus as implemented. Above about 100 cardinality, use fewer dimensions or move the analysis to a general-purpose system.
notes.explanation: That's well past the docs' own worked comparison: 10,000 nodes with node_filesystem_avail alone reaches only around 100,000 series, which is fine.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Do not overuse labels"

notes.front: To pick between a counter and a gauge, the rule of thumb is: if the value can {{c1::go down}}, it is a gauge.
notes.explanation: Counters can only go up, or reset (such as on a process restart), which is what makes rate() meaningful on them but never on a gauge.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Counter vs. gauge, summary vs. histogram"

notes.front: A metric tracks how many requests are currently in progress, a number that rises and falls. Counter or gauge?
notes.back: Gauge. It's a snapshot of current state that can go up and down, exactly the case the docs give a gauge for.
notes.explanation: A counter, by contrast, is for accumulating events or amounts, such as the total number of HTTP requests served.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Counter vs. gauge, summary vs. histogram"

notes.front: What does the docs' guidance recommend to avoid a time series that's absent until something first happens?
notes.back: Export a default value, such as 0, for any time series you know may exist in advance.
notes.explanation: Most client libraries, including Go, Java and Python, will do this automatically for metrics with no labels.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Avoid missing metrics"

notes.front: A counter for a labelled error type only appears once that error type first happens, making sum() over it awkward beforehand. What's the fix?
notes.back: Initialise that labelled counter to 0 in advance, so it exists as a time series before the error ever occurs.
notes.explanation: Time series that are absent until something happens are hard to work with, since the usual simple operations no longer suffice for them.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Avoid missing metrics"

notes.front: For code called more than 100k times a second, what does the docs' guidance suggest to limit instrumentation overhead?
notes.back: Limit the number of metrics updated in the inner loop, and avoid labels, or cache the result of the label lookup.
notes.explanation: Outside such performance-critical code, the resource cost of instrumentation is far outweighed by its benefits, so this caution doesn't generally apply.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Inner loops"

notes.front: What's the difference between an official and a third-party Prometheus exporter, as the exporters list marks them?
notes.back: Official exporters are maintained as part of the official Prometheus GitHub organization; others are externally contributed and maintained, commonly hosted elsewhere.
notes.explanation: The docs note they encourage more exporters being created, but cannot vet every third-party one for best practices.
notes.contrast: Official: e.g. Node exporter, Consul exporter, HAProxy exporter, listed as (official). Third-party: externally hosted, not vetted by the Prometheus project.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exporters and integrations, "Third-party exporters"

notes.front: Some software, such as Caddy or etcd, exposes metrics in the Prometheus format itself, marked "direct" in the docs' list. Does that software still need a separate exporter?
notes.back: No. No separate exporter is needed for software that already exposes Prometheus metrics directly.
notes.explanation: "Direct" here specifically means that software is also directly instrumented with a Prometheus client library, not just Prometheus-format output.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exporters and integrations, "Software exposing Prometheus metrics"

notes.front: If you find yourself wanting to apply the same label to all of an exporter's metrics, what does the writing-exporters guidance say to do?
notes.back: Stop. Labels like region or cluster name are target labels, and belong in Prometheus's scrape configs, not applied statically inside the exporter.
notes.explanation: It's not for the application to say where it fits in your label taxonomy; different people scraping the same application may name that taxonomy differently.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Writing exporters, "Target labels, not static scraped labels"

notes.front: An exporter's author wants every metric it exposes to carry a region="eu-west" label. Where should that label actually be set?
notes.back: In Prometheus's scrape configuration for that target, via service discovery, not baked into the exporter's own exposed metrics.
notes.explanation: region is exactly the kind of infrastructure-derived label the docs class as a target label rather than something the application should decide.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Writing exporters, "Target labels, not static scraped labels"

notes.front: If an exporter reports metrics about the scrape itself, such as how long it took, what metric type should those be, and how should they be named?
notes.back: Gauges, with the metric name prefixed by the exporter name, for example jmx_scrape_duration_seconds.
notes.explanation: Other scrape "meta" metrics, such as a counter of scrape count, should be avoided: they'd duplicate metrics Prometheus itself already generates automatically.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Writing exporters, "Metrics about the scrape itself"

notes.front: Exporters should not perform scrapes based on their own timers: all scrapes should be {{c1::synchronous}}, pulled only when Prometheus scrapes them.
notes.explanation: If you think you need to set your own timestamps on exposed metrics, the docs say you probably need the Pushgateway instead.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Writing exporters, "Scheduling"

notes.front: What are the two patterns the docs describe for handling a failed scrape, where the target application doesn't respond?
notes.back: Return a 5xx error, or expose a myexporter_up variable that's 0 or 1 depending on whether the scrape worked.
notes.explanation: The up-variable pattern is better when there are still some useful metrics to get even from a failed scrape, such as the exporter's own process stats.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Writing exporters, "Failed scrapes"

notes.front: The HAProxy exporter can still provide process stats even when a scrape of HAProxy itself fails. Which failed-scrape pattern fits better here: a 5xx error, or a myexporter_up variable?
notes.back: A myexporter_up variable, since a bare 5xx would throw away the still-useful process stats the exporter can report.
notes.explanation: The 5xx pattern is a little easier for users, since up works in the usual way, but with it you can't tell the exporter being down apart from the application being down.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Writing exporters, "Failed scrapes"

notes.front: Why does each Prometheus exporter get a unique default port number?
notes.back: A user may run many exporters and Prometheus components on the same machine, so unique ports make that easier.
notes.explanation: The allocations are tracked on a publicly editable wiki page, where authors may grab the next free port for a new exporter.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Writing exporters, "Port numbers"

notes.front: What pitfall arises from monitoring multiple instances through a single Pushgateway?
notes.back: The Pushgateway becomes both a single point of failure and a potential bottleneck.
notes.explanation: This is one of the reasons the docs limit recommended Pushgateway use so narrowly, rather than treating it as a general substitute for pulling.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, When to use the Pushgateway, "Should I be using the Pushgateway?"

notes.front: Using the Pushgateway means you lose Prometheus's automatic instance health monitoring via the {{c1::up}} metric.
notes.explanation: Prometheus scrapes the Pushgateway, not the jobs that pushed to it, so the up metric from each scrape describes the Pushgateway only.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, When to use the Pushgateway, "Should I be using the Pushgateway?"

notes.front: What does the Pushgateway do with a series once it's been pushed, unless something intervenes?
notes.back: It never forgets it, and exposes it to Prometheus forever unless that series is manually deleted via the Pushgateway's API.
notes.explanation: This is especially relevant when instances differentiate their metrics via an instance label: a renamed or removed instance's metrics stay stuck there.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, When to use the Pushgateway, "Should I be using the Pushgateway?"

notes.front: A batch job pushes metrics to the Pushgateway with instance="worker-3". That machine is later renamed and worker-3 no longer exists. Do worker-3's metrics disappear from the Pushgateway on their own?
notes.back: No. The Pushgateway never forgets pushed series, so worker-3's metrics stay exposed until someone deletes them manually via its API.
notes.explanation: With ordinary pull-style scraping, an instance's metrics would instead vanish automatically once it disappeared, which the Pushgateway doesn't do.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, When to use the Pushgateway, "Should I be using the Pushgateway?"

notes.front: Standard process metrics from client libraries carry the prefix {{c1::process_}}, such as process_cpu_seconds_total and process_resident_memory_bytes.
notes.explanation: If getting one of these values is impossible in a given language or runtime, client libraries should leave the metric out rather than export a bogus value.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Writing client libraries, "Process metrics"

notes.front: Besides process metrics, what else are client libraries encouraged to offer, with a prefix such as go_ or hotspot_?
notes.back: Runtime metrics: whatever makes sense for their language's own runtime, such as garbage collection statistics.
notes.explanation: Unlike the fixed process_ metrics, runtime metrics vary by language, since each runtime has its own things worth reporting.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Writing client libraries, "Runtime metrics"

notes.front: According to the naming guidance, what two things must a metric name refer to, singly rather than mixed?
notes.back: A single unit (don't mix seconds with milliseconds) and a single quantity (don't mix request size with request duration).
notes.explanation: As a rule of thumb, either sum() or avg() over all of a metric's dimensions should be meaningful; if it isn't, split it into separate metrics.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Metric names"

notes.front: A metric is named api_http_requests_create_total, with separate names for each operation, instead of one metric with an operation label. What problem does the naming guidance flag with this?
notes.back: Putting label names in the metric name introduces redundancy and causes confusion once the equivalent label is aggregated away.
notes.explanation: The guidance's own preferred version is api_http_requests_total with a label such as operation="create|update|delete".
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Labels"

notes.front: A metric name should have a {{c1::single-word application prefix}} relevant to the domain it belongs to, such as prometheus_notifications_total.
notes.explanation: Some metrics are more generic, like process_cpu_seconds_total, which uses a shared prefix exported by many client libraries rather than one specific application.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Metric names"

notes.front: A billing service exposes a metric simply named requests_total. What does the naming guidance say this name is missing?
notes.back: A single-word application prefix relevant to the metric's domain, such as billing_requests_total.
notes.explanation: Writing exporters guidance separately notes that requests_total on its own doesn't even say what kind of requests are being counted.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Metric names"

notes.front: What are two of the base units the naming guidance's table recommends for metrics, and the family each belongs to?
notes.back: Any two, e.g. seconds (time), bytes (bytes and bits), meters (length), celsius (temperature), volts (voltage), grams (mass), ratio (percent).
notes.explanation: The list is explicitly not exhaustive; it's a set of examples for common families, not a closed list of every possible unit.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Base Units"

notes.front: A network metric measures throughput in bits per second, since bits are the usual unit network engineers use. What base unit should the metric name use instead?
notes.back: bytes. The table specifically says to always use bytes, even where bits appear more common, to avoid confusion when combining different metrics.
notes.explanation: The table makes similar practical choices elsewhere, such as celsius over kelvin and grams over kilograms.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Base Units"

notes.front: For a percent value, the base unit table uses {{c1::ratio}}, with values expressed as 0–1 rather than 0–100.
notes.explanation: ratio is used only as a suffix for names like disk_usage_ratio, and the usual metric name pattern for this is A_per_B.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Base Units"

notes.front: What should a metric name's unit suffix look like, and what additional suffix does an accumulating count get?
notes.back: The unit suffix should be in plural form, and an accumulating counter additionally gets _total as a suffix.
notes.explanation: That's the pattern behind names like http_request_duration_seconds and process_cpu_seconds_total.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Metric names"

notes.front: A counter tracks a unit-less accumulating count of HTTP requests. Following the suffix rule, what should it be named, given there's no unit to add?
notes.back: http_requests_total. Even with no unit to append, the _total suffix marking it as an accumulating count still applies.
notes.explanation: Where a unit does apply to an accumulating count, both suffixes appear, as in process_cpu_seconds_total.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Metric names"

notes.front: What case convention do Prometheus metric and label names use?
notes.back: snake_case. Converting camelCase to snake_case is desirable, though automatic conversion doesn't always give nice results for names like myTCPExample.
notes.explanation: For those awkward cases, it's sometimes best to just leave the original name as-is rather than force an automatic conversion.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Metric names"; Writing exporters, "Naming"

notes.front: What does the naming guidance warn against storing in labels, giving user IDs and email addresses as examples?
notes.back: Dimensions with high cardinality, i.e. many different label values, since every unique combination of label values is a new time series.
notes.explanation: Unbounded sets of values like these are exactly what dramatically increases the amount of data stored.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Labels"

notes.front: A metric adds an email label holding each user's own email address. What does the naming guidance say is wrong with this?
notes.back: Email addresses are an unbounded, high-cardinality set of values, exactly what the guidance says not to store as a label.
notes.explanation: Each distinct email value creates its own time series, so this one label alone could add an unbounded number of series.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Labels"

notes.front: A team wants to add a running binary's version string onto its request-count series, without adding a high-cardinality version label directly to that series. Which function reaches for a separate info metric to do this?
notes.back: info(), which finds matching info series and adds their non-identifying (data) labels onto the target series at query time.
notes.explanation: foobar_build_info is the naming guide’s example of a pseudo-metric carrying metadata about the running binary. info() is experimental and needs --enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Functions, "info()"

notes.front: Besides collection duration, what else does the docs' guidance recommend a non-trivial custom collector export as a gauge?
notes.back: The number of errors encountered during that collection.
notes.explanation: Both this and the duration gauge describe just the one collection they came from, which is why gauges, not histograms, fit here.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "Collectors"

notes.front: A nightly job that doesn't run continuously and completes in a few minutes, with nobody waiting on it: which of the three service types does this fit best?
notes.back: A batch job, distinguished from offline processing precisely by not running continuously, which is what makes scraping it difficult.
notes.explanation: If the same job instead ran continuously in the background, it would be better described as offline processing, or online-serving if something waited on each result.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Instrumentation, "The three types of services"

notes.front: A metric is named httpRequestDurationSeconds, following the camelCase style of its host language. Should it be renamed for Prometheus?
notes.back: Yes, generally to http_request_duration_seconds, since Prometheus metric and label names use snake_case.
notes.explanation: Automatic camelCase-to-snake_case conversion doesn't always read well for names like myTCPExample, so such awkward cases may be left as-is instead.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Metric names"

notes.front: A monitored system is a black box that can't run any extra code on it at all, such as a network device managed purely over its own protocol. Can it expose Prometheus metrics directly, or does it need an exporter?
notes.back: It needs an exporter, since it can't be directly instrumented or run software that already speaks the Prometheus format.
notes.explanation: Everything under “Software exposing Prometheus metrics” needs no separate exporter, whether or not it is marked “direct”; that marker only means the software is also directly instrumented with a Prometheus client library.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exporters and integrations, "Software exposing Prometheus metrics"

notes.front: A team wants to scrape MySQL metrics and is choosing between mysqld_exporter, marked (official), and an unrelated community fork. Which one is maintained as part of the official Prometheus GitHub organization?
notes.back: mysqld_exporter, since the (official) marker specifically means it's maintained under the official Prometheus GitHub organization.
notes.explanation: That marker says nothing about the fork's quality either way; it only tells you where an exporter is maintained.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exporters and integrations, "Third-party exporters"

notes.front: What may a metric name's components be ordered by, to keep related metrics grouped together?
notes.back: It may put common name components first, so that a lexicographically sorted list of metric names groups related metrics together.
notes.explanation: The docs give prometheus_tsdb_head_truncations_closed_total as this style, versus prometheus_tsdb_head_closed_truncations_total, which reads more naturally per metric but sorts less tidily.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Metric names"

notes.front: A metric is named go_goroutines, describing something specific to the Go runtime rather than the operating-system process. Is this a process metric or a runtime metric?
notes.back: A runtime metric: it carries the go_ prefix, not process_, because it's specific to that language's own runtime rather than the operating-system process in general.
notes.explanation: Process metrics all share the fixed process_ prefix; runtime metrics instead use whatever prefix suits the language, such as go_ or hotspot_.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Writing client libraries, "Runtime metrics"

notes.front: A team is deciding between a single api_request_duration_seconds metric with a stage label, or three separate metrics for extract, transform and load. Which fits the guidance to use labels?
notes.back: The single metric with a stage label, e.g. stage="extract|transform|load", following the same pattern the docs give for request stages.
notes.explanation: One labelled metric can be summed, averaged or graphed as a whole, which three separately named metrics can't be as easily.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Metric and label naming, "Labels"
